title-group.article-title: One-step Design of Potent and Non-hemolytic Antimicrobial Peptides by Using a Database-guided, Non-machine Learning Approach

abstract.p: The search for antibiotics is urgent because of the global antibiotic resistance problem. While a variety of strategies are actively sought, interest in antimicrobial peptides persists due to high potency and low chance of resistance development. The establishment of the antimicrobial peptide database laid the foundation for peptide prediction and design. Both artificial intelligence and non-AI approaches have been demonstrated. Since AI remains a black box and does not teach us how to design peptide antibiotics, this study took a database-guided approach. Our peptide design benefited from the recent classification of peptides into hemolytic and non-hemolytic groups in the APD6. Our designed peptides rapidly killed Gram-negative bacteria Escherichia coli and Acinetobacter baumannii, but not Gram-positive methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, Staphylococcus epidermidis, and Bacillus subtilis. In addition, our peptide inhibited bacterial attachment, biofilm formation, and disrupted preformed biofilms. Remarkably, YZ200, designed based on the non-hemolytic group, showed no sign of hemolysis even at 400 μM, whereas YZ201, designed based on the hemolytic group, displayed toxicity. Our analysis uncovered a higher hydrophobic ratio for the hemolytic group. Mechanistic studies revealed that the peptide permeabilized and depolarized bacterial membranes. The predicted membrane-bound structure of YZ200 contains a longer amphipathic helix, explaining its higher potency than YZ201. By comparing our experimental results for the designed peptides with AI-predicted activity and toxicity outcomes, it becomes evident that great progress has been made for AI prediction of antimicrobial peptides and such predictions will be improved in the future by including good data as illustrated herein.

body.p: One of the greatest achievements in human history is the serendipitous discovery of penicillin by Alexander Fleming who won Nobel prize 80 years ago.1 As warned by Fleming, bacteria can fight back by developing resistance. He is correct as antibiotic resistance has become a global issue today! One useful strategy to handle global antibiotic resistance crisis is to search for novel potent candidates either from natural sources or via knowledge-based design, including the use of artificial intelligence (AI). Investigators show continued interest in antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) because these peptides can rapidly and effectively eliminate antibiotic-resistant pathogens.2–5 The amphipathic helical peptides, such as magainin, cecropin, and human cathelicidin LL-37, have been extensively studied.6–8 The cationic nature of these peptides allowed them to recognize and damage anionic membranes of bacteria by forming pores. Such a membrane-disrupting effect is so powerful that these AMPs leave a minimal chance for bacteria to develop resistance.2,5 As a consequence, many peptide analogs have been designed based on these natural templates. Some modified or natural candidates such as magainin and LL-37 have been tested in clinical settings.9,10 Other approaches, such as structure-based design and peptide library screen, have also been utilized to identify novel AMPs.11–15

To facilitate antibiotic design, Wang lab established the antimicrobial peptide database (APD).16–20 Our hope is that, by registering natural AMPs isolated from the six life kingdoms (bacteria, archaea, protists, fungi, plants, and animals) into the APD, we can learn the design principles of AMPs from nature. This knowledge can then be harnessed to design peptides with desired properties. This requires a careful classification of natural AMPs based on their functions, including antibacterial, antifungal, antiviral, antiparasitic, anticancer, anti-diabetes, anti-endotoxin, antioxidant, anti-biofilm, wound healing, immune regulation, and so on.20 Each functional class on the Wheel of Function then becomes a starting point for peptide discovery. It is also necessary to classify the peptides based on their structures. The APD has unified AMPs into four self-consistent classes: α-helix, β-sheet, mixed α-helix and β-sheet (i.e., αβ), and non-αβ structures.20 These well-annotated structure-activity data in the APD laid the foundation for both peptide design and predictions by a variety of approaches (Graphic). Both single-label and multi-label machine learning and deep learning predictions were demonstrated.21–29 A single-label prediction only predicts one property (e.g., antimicrobial activity or hemolysis) at a time, while a multi-label approach can predict multiple peptide activities such as antibacterial, antifungal and antiviral effects. These AI predictions greatly accelerated the identification of potential antimicrobial sequences.28,29 One shortcoming of current AI approaches, however, is that such predictions work like a black box and do not provide insight into peptide design. To improve our understanding of AMPs, this study took a non-AI approach. These non-AI peptide design approaches include template-based design, the grammar approach, database screening, and database filtering technology.30–38 The database filtering technology33 is powerful and inspiring. The first filter enables the selection of a set of AMPs with a desired activity (e.g., anti-Gram-positive bacteria, antifungal, antiviral). Subsequent filters can be assembled into a pipeline to extract the optimal peptide parameters by applying the most probable principle at each step. Our selection of anti-Gram+ AMPs in our previous design was successful since the designed peptide DFTamP1 killed Gram-positive methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) USA300 but not Gram-negative Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas aeruginosa.33 This database method has been utilized to design peptides against Gram-negative bacteria, fungi, and viruses as well.34,37,38 The above designed peptides, however, may be toxic and require additional optimization step to mitigate peptide toxicity.39

We hypothesize that potent and non-toxic peptides may be designed in one step if we can start from a good data set containing AMPs that are not hemolytic. This is clearly desired in terms of the R&D cost. For our purpose, AMPs in the APD6 are classified into hemolytic (HC50, 50% hemolytic concentration < 100 μM) and non-hemolytic groups (HC50 > 100 μM).17 Our selection of a HC50 greater than 100 μM is to ensure that a potent peptide (MIC < 10 μM) has a cell selectivity value (HC50/MIC) at least 10-fold higher than the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC). Different from our previous most probable design,33 here we designed two novel peptides by making use of the unexplored average peptide parameter space from either hemolytic or non-hemolytic groups. With the designed peptide sequences in hand, we then predicted peptide antibacterial activity using three machine learning programs available online. We also tested three platforms for peptide toxicity prediction. Subsequently, we validated peptide activity using a panel of bacteria, including antibiotic-resistant clinical strains. In addition, we evaluated peptide toxicity using different mammalian cell lines. Based on our results, we further probed peptide mechanism of action and investigated its antibiofilm capability. Our results proved the concept that the non-hemolytic peptide data set in our database is indeed a good starting place for designing potent and selective peptides. Our comparison of experimental and predicted results reveals a need for future improvement of AI prediction of antimicrobial peptides.

sec.title: Peptide Design and Parameter Calculations.
sec.p: We started our design by selecting all anti-MRSA peptides in the APD (254 in March 2023).17 This set of peptides was then filtered to obtain hemolytic and non-hemolytic peptides. The hemolytic peptides have been annotated in the APD since version 1.16 This led to 29 peptides. The non-hemolytic peptides were newly generated in the APD based on our definition (HC50 > 100 μM). They could be searched in the “Additional Information” field by entering the search term “hemo.lytic”.17 We obtained 18 non-hemolytic peptides for our design. Next, we calculated the average amino acid compositions for these two peptide groups by using the APD statistical tool. These data sheets (Figures S1 and S2) are provided as supporting information. In the APD, the 20 amino acids are separated into four groups: (1) hydrophobic (I, V, L, F, C, M, A, and W), (2) GP (G and P), (3) polar (T, S, Y, Q, and N), and (4) charged amino acids (E, D, H, K, and R).16 The percentages for all amino acids in each class were then summed (Table 1). Meanwhile, the averaged peptide length, 21, in the calculated data sheets (Figures S1 and S2) was also taken for peptide design. The multiplication of the amino acid percentage in each group with peptide length produced the number of amino acids for each group (Table 1). After rounding up, the sum of these amino acids equals to peptide length. Since amino acid diversification gave some advantage,37 we then partitioned the total amino acids in each group to major amino acids there with higher percentages. The amino acid composition is also provided in Table 1. Finally, we arranged these amino acids into an amphipathic pattern XXLLXXLLXXLLXXLXXXLLX where L is hydrophobic and X is hydrophilic amino acid. In this way we designed YZ200. It is evident that the amino acid composition in Table 1 could produce a library of peptides. For simplicity, we designed only one peptide here to prove the principle. By following the same procedure, we also designed YZ201 based on the statistical information calculated for hemolytic peptides (Table 1). Compared to YZ200, YZ201 contains one more leucine and phenylalanine but one less arginine and glycine.

Based on the peptide sequences, we accessed the APD to calculate peptide properties and entered them in Table 2. YZ200 and YZ201 share the same peptide length but differ in net charge, hydrophobic ratio,16 GRAVY,40 and Boman index (i.e., protein-binding potential).7 While YZ200 contains one additional basic amino acid, YZ201 is more hydrophobic (52% vs. 43%), consistent with a more positive GRAVY value. Boman index provides essentially the same information except for the reversal in sign: more hydrophobic peptides have a negative value whereas basic peptides show a positive value (Table 2). By using the sequence alignment program in the APD, we found that the sequences of YZ200 and YZ201 are 43.5% and 47.8% similar to that of the amphibian peptide PGLa-AN2, which is active against E. coli (MIC 25 μM) and S. aureus (MIC 100 μM).41

sec.title: AI Prediction of Antibacterial Activity and Toxicity of Newly Designed Peptides.
sec.p: The construction of the APD also facilitated the development of machine learning prediction methods for AMPs.28,29 Here we predicted antibacterial activity for both YZ200 and YZ201 using three antibacterial programs available online. All the programs predicted that both designed peptides are AMPs. While no difference could be seen from the prediction of the anti-BP website,21 AMPfun predicted slightly higher probability for YZ201 (0.9486) than YZ200 (0.9328).23 However, AMP scanner, a deep learning prediction,24 revealed a significant difference in the likelihood of being antibacterial (YZ200: 0.9972 vs. YZ201: 0.5712) (Table 2). In all the cases, 1.0 means a 100% chance to be an AMP. It is clear these programs do not provide consistent results.

We also employed three online tools to predict the likelihood of peptide hemolysis or being toxin and the results are also provided in Table 2. HemoPred25 predicted that both YZ200 and YZ201 are hemolytic. In contrast, HAPPENN26 found that both peptides have a low hemolytic tendency (0.112 and 0.325) although YZ201 is slightly more hemolytic than YZ200. In this scale, 0 implies no hemolysis and 1 means 100% hemolysis. A third program was created to predict whether the peptide is a toxin.27 Both peptides were predicted as non-toxin. Evidently, these toxicity prediction programs did not provide consensus results, either. Which prediction is close to the truth remains to be validated.

sec.title: Experimental Proof 1: Antimicrobial Activity of the Designed Peptides.
sec.p: To measure antibacterial activity of the designed peptides, we utilized the standard microdilution assay in Mueller Hinton Broth (MHB) as described previously.15 To better delineate peptide activity spectrum, we included three Gram-positive bacteria: Bacillus subtillis 168, Staphylococcus epidermidis 1457, and Staphylococcus aureus USA300 LAC (MRSA) and three extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Gram-negative bacterial strains (P. aeruginosa, E. coli, and K. pneumonia), and one clinical strain A. baumannii. Both YZ200 (MIC 2–4 μM) and YZ201 (MIC 4–8 μM) demonstrated excellent activity against A. baumannii and E. coli and moderate activity against K. pneumoniae (32 μM for YZ200 and 8–16 μM for YZ201). In addition, YZ200 was able to inhibit other strains of E. coli equally well (Table 3). However, the newly designed peptides were unable to inhibit P. aeruginosa (MIC > 32 μM) and S. aureus USA300 (MIC > 32 μM). Both peptides remained inactive against MRSA even at 128 μM (Table 3). As a positive control, colistin eliminated all the tested Gram-negative pathogens but not MRSA. Hence, YZ200 peptides have a different activity spectrum from 17BIPHE2, a human cathelicidin LL-37 engineered peptide,42 which shows broad-spectrum activity against both Gram-positive and negative pathogens (Table 3).

sec.title: Experimental proof 2: Cytotoxicity of the Designed Peptides.
sec.p: We then evaluated the toxicity profile of the peptides using different mammalian cells. Hemolytic assays showed that, similar to colistin, YZ200 did not lyse human red blood cells even at 400 μM, indicating high cell selectivity (Figure 1A). YZ201 induced low-level, dose-dependent hemolysis only at high concentrations (200–400 μM), resulting in 10%−27% hemolysis. The HC50 values of both peptides were significantly higher than 400 μM. Both designed peptides are less hemolytic than 17BIPHE2.42

To further characterize cytotoxicity, we also used human skin keratinocytes (HaCaT) and human liver cancer cells (HepG2). Similar to colistin, YZ200 appeared to be non-toxic to both cell lines at the highest concentration tested (Figures 1B and 1C). In contrast, YZ201 exhibited marked toxicity, with HC50 values around 100 μM in HaCaT cells (Figure 1B) and 57 μM in HepG2 cells (Figure 1C). Notably, YZ201 caused a dose-dependent reduction in HepG2 cell viability, with near 0% viability at 100 μM. These results suggest that YZ200 is relatively safe at the MIC values required to kill E. coli and A. baumannii (Table 3). They also indicate that YZ200, designed based on a non-hemolytic data set, was indeed not toxic to three mammalian cell lines, whereas YZ201, designed based on a hemolytic data set, showed a dose-dependent toxicity. Thus, we conducted additional studies using YZ200.

sec.title: Effects of pH, Salts, and Serum on YZ200 Activity.
sec.p: To further understand the antimicrobial potential of YZ200, we evaluated the effects of pH, physiological salts, and human serum on peptide activity. YZ200 retained its activity against E. coli under both acidic (pH 6.4) and basic (pH 8.2) conditions, but the MIC increased 2- to 4-fold against A. baumannii at pH 8.2 (Table 4). In the presence of different concentrations of NaCl (75 mM, 150 mM, and 300 mM), YZ200 remained active against E. coli at 75 mM, but started to lose activity at higher salt concentrations. Likewise, this peptide also showed reduced activity against A. baumannii with an increase in salt concentration. Of note, 17BIPHE2, a positive control, remained largely active against both bacterial strains under various conditions.

sec.title: Growth Inhibition, Killing Kinetics, and Mechanism of Action.
sec.p: We then investigated the growth inhibition kinetics of YZ200 against E. coli at varying concentrations. YZ200 completely inhibited E. coli growth at a concentration of 2 μM (Figure 1D). However, for A. baumannii, complete inhibition was not achieved until 4 μM (Figure 1E). Such inhibition curves are consistent with the MIC values for these peptides against these strains (Table 3). Given that YZ200 is more effective against E. coli, we compared its bacterial killing kinetics. At 2× MIC, YZ200 eliminated E. coli in 120 minutes, whereas colistin achieved this in 30 minutes (Figure S3).

sec.title: Mechanism of action of the designed peptides.
sec.p: We also investigated the possible mechanism of action of YZ200. Using propidium iodide (PI) as a probe, YZ200 (at MIC) caused an increase in fluorescence, implying membrane permeabilization of both E. coli (Figure 1F) and A. baumannii (Figure 1G). It appears that YZ200 demonstrated stronger membrane permeabilization potential than colistin at the MIC. We then studied the membrane depolarizing potential of YZ200 at 1× MIC (2 μM for E. coli E423–17 and 4 μM for A. baumannii B28–16) in PBS buffer primed with glucose. YZ200 was found to be more effective in membrane depolarization than colistin, though less effective than the positive control Triton-X100 against both bacterial strains (Figures 1H and 1I).

sec.title: Structural insight into antimicrobial potency against Gram-negative bacteria.
sec.p: To understand the structure-activity relationship, we also predicted peptide three-dimensional structures using a state-of-the-art program. We selected PEP-FOLD since it has achieved similar accuracy to AlphaFold43 with better performance on small peptides with 5–50 amino acids. Based on structural knowledge on linear AMPs, we assume that the predicted structure represents membrane-bound form because such peptides usually do not have any structure in aqueous solution. Using PEP-FOLD3, YZ200 was predicted entirely helical (Figure 2A), while YZ201 had a helical region spanning residues 2–14 (Figure 2B). We also made use of the most recent version of PEP-FOLD4.44 The most probable structures were predicted similarly for YZ200 (Figure 2C) but a slightly longer helix (residues 2–16) was found for YZ201 (Figure 2D). The structural difference between YZ200 and YZ201 provides one possible explanation for slightly higher activity of YZ200 (Table 3) since a longer amphipathic helix can better associate with bacterial membranes. We have observed this phenomenon in multiple cases. A bacterial membrane anchor, with a short three-turn amphipathic helix (10 residues), was not bactericidal. Extending the helix by one turn (13 residues) made the peptide antibacterial.30 In the case of human LL-37, shortening the helix by removing hydrophobic amino acids from both termini of the major antimicrobial peptide GF-17 (17 residues) led to KR-12 (12 amino acids), the minimal antibacterial peptide, which has a shorter helix and becomes less active than GF-17.12 In addition to helix length, YZ200 has one extra basic charge, which is important to target the anionic membranes of Gram-negative pathogens. The structure of YZ201 is fascinating with the C-terminal aromatic ring of F21 bending toward the hydrophobic surface of the amphipathic helix, presumably enhancing bacterial membrane binding. There is a precedent where an N-terminal tyrosine aromatic ring of a human apolipoprotein A-I fragment also bends toward the hydrophobic surface of the amphipathic helix determined by 2D NMR spectroscopy.45

sec.title: Antibiofilm activity of YZ200.
sec.p: Biofilm formation on medical implants poses a challenging task. Because the outside of biofilms may be coated with polysaccharides, DNA, and proteins, bacteria in biofilms can dodge immune attack. Biofilms are also resistant to conventional antibiotics. Hence, we tested the capability of our designed cationic peptide YZ200 in inhibiting bacterial attachment, biofilm formation, and disruption of preformed biofilms. Surface attachment is crucial for initial biofilm formation. Treatment with YZ200 at various folds of MIC resulted in ~40% inhibition of E. coli attachment (Figure 3A). While colistin achieved a similar effect at 4 × MIC or below, it more effectively inhibited bacterial attachment at 8 × MIC (Figure 3B). However, YZ200 appeared to be more effective in inhibiting the attachment of A. baumannii in a concentration-dependent manner, inhibiting about 90% attachment following treatment with 8 × MIC (Figure 3C). As a positive control, colistin similarly inhibited the attachment of A. baumannii as well in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 3D). Additionally, YZ200 (1× MIC and 2× MIC) could effectively inhibit biofilm formation of both E. coli and A. baumannii at MIC or above (Figures 3E and 3G). The inhibition of biofilm formation by YZ200 was comparable to colistin against E. coli and slightly less effective in the case of A. baumannii (Figures 3F and 3H). Finally, YZ200 disrupted approximately 50% of 5-day preformed E. coli biofilms at various MIC folds (2×, 4×, and 8× MIC) (Figure 3I), while colistin eliminated 75% of the preformed biofilm at high concentrations (4× and 8× MIC) (Figure 3J). Both YZ200 and colistin also displayed a disruptive effect on preformed A. baumannii biofilms, with 40–50% biofilms left at 8× MIC (Figure 3K & 3L). All these experiments indicate that our designed peptide YZ200 possesses antibiofilm ability.

sec.title: Comparison of experimental results of database-designed peptides with AI predictions.
sec.p: In the antimicrobial peptide field, the amphipathic model is widely accepted as a general guide for peptide design and improvement.2–4,7,17 Earlier reductionist design consolidated this idea by designing amphipathic LK peptides using only leucine and lysine to represent hydrophobic and hydrophilic amino acids, respectively.46 The construction of the APD enabled the development of new methods for peptide design and prediction. Statistical results led to the identification of frequently occurring amino acids in a group of peptides from different sources, with different structures, and activities.18 In amphibians, residues leucine, alanine, glycine, and lysine are such amino acids. Hence, this database finding has endowed significance to the initial selection of leucine and lysine for designing LK peptides. However, LK-peptides tend to be hemolytic probably due to richness (>25%) in both leucine and lysine. Intriguingly, no natural AMPs in the APD are simultaneously rich in these two amino acids.47 Our previous study reported that a decrease in hydrophobic amino acids can reduce peptide hemolysis.42 Consistent with this finding, we found in this study that YZ201 is indeed more hydrophobic (52%) than non-hemolytic YZ200 (43% in Table 2). In the current APD6 as of November 2025, 439 hemolytic peptides shared an average hydrophobic content of 51.4%. In contrast, 779 non-hemolytic peptides possessed a hydrophobic content of 44.45% (instruction for sequence download is included in Figure S4 of the supporting information). Notably, leucine is higher in hemolytic peptides (leucine 14.81%), but lower in non-hemolytic AMPs (leucine 12.03%). However, net charge on average is higher in non-hemolytic peptides (+4.76) and lower in hemolytic peptides (+3.54). Notably, our hemolytic results for YZ200 and YZ201 did not support the predicted outcome of HemoPred,25 which suggests that both YZ200 and YZ201 are hemolytic. In contrast, HAPPENN26 (Table 2) predicted low levels of hemolysis for both peptides with YZ200 less hemolytic than YZ201. Experimentally, YZ200 is not hemolytic even till 400 μM, and YZ201 only started to show hemolysis at higher peptide concentrations. Hence, the overall prediction of HAPPEN is rather good in this particular case. Unlike AI predictions which behave like a black box, our database-aided design provides statistical insight into the molecular basis for hemolysis of AMPs where higher hydrophobic ratios (defined in the Table 2 legend) constitute a key determinant. This observation is informative considering numerous factors that could influence the results of hemolysis such as blood cell types and evaluation conditions.

It is interesting that our designed peptides killed only Gram-negative E. coli and A. baumannii but not Gram-positive MRSA (MIC > 128 μM). This may result from our use of average amino acid composition for the peptide ensemble in our peptide design. In other words, amino acid averaging of various anti-MRSA peptides has generated a different peptide parameter space not represented by the starting candidates in the group. Such an activity spectrum of YZ200 and YZ201 is opposite to that of the DFTamP1 peptide which was designed based on the most probable parameters derived from the anti-Gram+ bacteria, thereby effectively killing Gram-positive MRSA but not Gram-negative bacteria.33 Since our designed peptides are amphipathic (Figure 2), it is not surprising that all the AI prediction programs21–23 we used here were able to predict YZ200 and YZ201 as antibacterial peptides (Table 2). Among these predictions, the deep learning predictions from AMP scanner,24 trained based on the APD data,18 suggest a higher antibacterial probability for YZ200 than YZ201, consistent with measured lower MIC values for YZ200 against E. coli and A. baumannii. This underscores the power of this AI program. To gain further insight into the accuracy of AMP scanner,24 we uploaded 99 AI predicted activity-validated AMPs recently registered in the APD6 and obtained a prediction accuracy of 77.7% when tested using the version 1 program (trained around 2018) and a prediction accuracy of 87% when using version 2 model (trained January 2025). It is likely that version 1 training did not include most of the AI-predicted peptides collected into the APD more recently, while version 2 Scanner training based on the APD might have included about 75% of the sequences we tested. Hence, there is still room to improve the prediction accuracy of AMP Scanner. Based on various activities annotated in the APD, computing scientists have also attempted to make multiple label predictions (e.g., antibacterial, antiviral, anticancer, and antifungal activities).22 We then tested one of the multi-label predictors available online. AMPfun produced slightly higher scores for Gram-positive (0.78–0.88) than Gram-negative activities (0.67–0.79).23 Experimentally, both YZ200 and YZ201 primarily killed Gram-negative bacteria. YZ200 did not inhibit the three Gram-positive bacteria we tested even at 128 μM (Table 3). This disagreement between experimental and predicted results underscores the requirement of additional studies to improve the prediction accuracy of bacterial Gram type. For instance, the APD6 proposes data filtering to remove unreliable peptides (i.e. noise) when their activity spectra (Gram+ vs. Gram-) have not been sufficiently defined.19

Future studies may combine database design with AI prediction to screen more peptide candidates. Our designed peptide YZ200, with high potency against Gram-negative bacteria and no observed hemolysis even at 400 μM, is a promising candidate for future development. The peptide may be engineered by incorporating non-standard amino acids or by introducing stapled bonds to increase its stability to proteases. Peptide stability can be evaluated in human serum or in vivo via pharmacokinetic studies. We can then test peptide toxicity in vitro and in vivo as well. Finally, peptide in vivo efficacy may be evaluated using topical and systemic murine models. While in vivo antibiofilm capability can be tested in wound models, systemic efficacy can be evaluated using neutropenic mice. All animal studies must be approved by Institution Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC). These future studies are critical to advance this promising peptide toward clinical applications.

sec.title: CONCLUSIONS
sec.p: Novel antibiotics are urgently needed for the sustainability of our society. This study illustrates the accelerated design of highly potent and non-toxic antimicrobial peptides in a single step. Our design was made possible due to our recent definition and data annotation in the APD of hemolytic and non-hemolytic groups.17 The use of a good data set of non-hemolytic AMPs offered a great advantage since the designed peptide YZ200 is not only non-toxic to multiple cell lines (no hemolysis at 400 μM) but also potent against E. coli and A. baumannii (MIC 2–4 μM). The non-hemolytic property of YZ200 can be attributed to the lower hydrophobic ratio of the non-hemolytic data set than the hemolytic data set for YZ201 design. The higher antibacterial activity of YZ200 than YZ201 is consistent with a longer amphipathic structure predicted for YZ200, enabling membrane targeting. The APD also laid the foundation for AI prediction of AMPs.28,29 We tested three machine learning prediction platforms available online and found that the quantitative results from AMPscanner24 agreed better with the determined activities for YZ200 and YZ201. Among three hemolytic/toxic predictors we tested, the closest prediction was made by HAPPENN.26 It appears that AI prediction of AMPs has made outstanding progress. By combining good data with powerful algorithms, we anticipate that the accuracy of AI prediction will continue to improve. However, other non-AI peptide design methods as illustrated here and previously (see Graphic) should not be abandoned in search of novel peptide antibiotics. The high potency and low toxicity of YZ200 justifies its future development through detailed in vivo stability, toxicity, and efficacy studies.

sec.title: Chemicals.
sec.p: All the chemicals were purchased from established vendors such as Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc and MilliporeSigma. Peptides were made by Genemed Synthesis, Inc. (San Antonio, TX). All the peptides were > 95% pure based on HPLC. The correct mass of each peptide was validated by Mass Spectrometry. Since these peptides do not contain tryptophan, they were quantitated by measuring UV absorbance differences between 215 and 225 nm based on the Waddell’s method.48

sec.title: Antibacterial Assay.
sec.p: Bacteria used in this study include Staphylococcus aureus USA300 LAC, Staphylococcus epidermidis 1457, Bacillus subtilis 168, Pseudomonas aeruginosa E411–17, Klebsiella pneumoniae E406–17, Acinetobacter baumannii B28–16, Escherichia coli E423–17, E. coli E416–17, E. coli K-12, E. coli ATCC 25922, and E. coli ATCC 35128. Peptide activity was tested using the established lab protocol as described previously.39 In brief, a peptide concentration gradient with twofold dilution was made in the 96-well polystyrene microplate at 10 μL per well. Bacteria were grown to the exponential phase, diluted to ~105 CFU/mL in MHB, and partitioned into the 96-well microplate at 90 μL per well. The microplates were incubated at 37°C overnight and read on a ChroMate 4300 Microplate Reader at 600 nm (GMI, Ramsey, MN). The peptide concentration in wells without bacterial growth is the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC). As the convention, MIC values were represented as ranges.

To evaluate pH effects on peptide activity, the pH of the media was adjusted to a targeted value for autoclave and then remeasured at room temperature. For salt and serum effects on peptide activity, stock NaCl solution or human serum were added to the media.

sec.title: Bacterial Growth Curves.
sec.p: E. coli E423–17 or A. baumannii B28–16 was grown to the exponential phase (OD600 ~ 0.3) in MHB. The culture was diluted to ~105 CFU/mL. One hundred eighty microliters of bacterial suspension were then mixed with the peptide (20 μL) and incubated at 37°C for 24 h. The plate was incubated at 37 °C with continuous shaking in a FLUOstar Omega (BMG LABTECH, NC) microplate reader. The sample was read every 5 min for 24 h at a wavelength of 600 nm.

sec.title: Killing Kinetics.
sec.p: E. coli E423–17 was re-grown to the exponential phase in MHB. The culture was diluted to ~105 CFU/mL. One milliliter of bacterial suspension was then mixed with YZ200 or colistin at 2× MIC and incubated at 37°C. After 15, 30, 60, 90, and 120 min incubation, 50 μL was taken and serially diluted with 1×PBS and plated on MH Agar plates. The plates were incubated overnight at 37°C for bacterial CFU determination.

sec.title: Hemolytic Assay.
sec.p: The hemolytic effects of peptides were evaluated using a previous method.39 In brief, human red blood cells (hRBCs, UNMC Blood Bank) were washed (3×) and diluted to 2% using the saline solution. Aliquots of 90 μL were mixed with 10 μL of serially diluted peptide solutions. After incubation at 37°C for 1 h, plates were centrifuged at 500g for 5 min and aliquots of the supernatant were transferred to a new 96-well microplate to measure the amount of hemoglobin released at 545 nm (relative to 1% Triton X-100) using a ChroMate Microplate Reader.

sec.title: Cytotoxicity Assay Using Other Human Cell Lines.
sec.p: The cytotoxic effects of peptides were evaluated using an established procedure.49 Human keratinocytes HaCaT cells were grown in Dulbecco’s Modification of Eagles’s Medium/High Glucose (DMEM, Hyclone, UT) containing 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) (Mediatech, Corning, Manassas, VA). HepG2 cells were cultured in ATCC-formulated Eagle’s Minimum Essential Medium with 10% FBS. Cells were grown at 37°C in 5% CO2, and the medium was changed every other day. Peptides were diluted in a 96-well polystyrene microplate (10 μL each well) and mixed with 90 μL of cell suspensions (105 cells/mL) in their respective media. The mixture was incubated at 37°C in a 5% CO2 for 24 h. Then, 20 μL of MTS reagent (MTS cell proliferation assay kit, Promega, WI) was added to each well and incubated at 37 °C for 2 h. The absorbance was determined at 492 nm using a microplate reader. The percentage viability was determined using the following formula: Percentage viability = (OD value of treated cells/OD value of untreated cells) × 100, where OD is the optical density.

sec.title: Bacterial Membrane Permeabilization.
sec.p: The membrane permeation experiment was conducted as described.39 The peptide ladder was prepared as described for the antibacterial assay with 10 μL in a black COSTAR 96-well plate. Propidium iodide (PI) (MP Biomedicals, Solon, OH) was dissolved in DMSO (Thermo Fisher Scientific, NY) to 20 mM. This PI stock solution was further diluted to 1 mM with water and 2 μL of 1 mM PI was added to each well. Exponential phase E. coli E423–17 or A. baumannii B28–16 was diluted to OD600 0.11 with tryptic soy broth (TSB) and 88 μL was added to each well. Colistin was used as the positive control and gentamicin as the negative control. The plate was incubated at 37 °C with continuous shaking in a FLUOstar Omega (BMG LABTECH, NC) microplate reader. The sample was read every 5 min for 24 cycles with excitation and emission wavelengths at 584 nm and 620 nm, respectively.

sec.title: Bacterial Membrane Depolarization.
sec.p: Membrane depolarization was conducted as described.39 In brief, an overnight culture of E. coli E423–17 or A. baumannii B28–16 was inoculated into TSB and grown to the exponential phase. Bacteria were washed with 1×PBS, re-suspended in twice the volume of 1×PBS containing 25 mM glucose, and incubated at 37°C for 15 min. Then, 500 nM (final concentration) of the DiBAC4 (3) bis-(1, 3-dibutylbarbituric acid) trimethine oxonol (ANASPEC, CA) was added and vortexed gently. Aliquots of 90 μL of the energized bacteria solution were loaded to the 96 well plates (Corning COSTAR, AZ) and placed in a FLUOstar Omega microplate reader (BMG LABTECH, NC). Fluorescence was read for 15 min at excitation and emission wavelengths of 485 nm and 520 nm, respectively. Then, 10 μL of the peptide solution was added and fluorescence readings were recorded for 40 min. Triton X-100 (0.1%) was used as a positive control and untreated sample as negative control.

sec.title: Antibiofilm Experiments.
sec.p: Three experiments were conducted as described.50 Frist, inhibition of bacterial attachment. In brief, an overnight culture of E. coli E423–17 or A. baumannii B28–16 was grown overnight in TSB media. Then, 180 μL of this culture were added to each well of the microtiter plates containing 20 μL of various MIC folds (1×, 2×, 4×, and 8× MIC) of YZ200 or colistin. The plates were then incubated at 37°C for 1 h. Next, media was aspirated, washed with 1× PBS, and 200 μL of TSB containing XTT 10% [2, 3-bis (2-methyloxy-4-nitro-5-sulfophenyl)-2H-tertazolium-5-carboxanilide] (ATCC, VA, USA) solution was added. After incubation at 37°C for 2 h, absorbance was read at 450 nm using a ChromateTM microtiter plate reader. TSB containing 10% XTT served as blank, while bacterial culture treated with water served as a positive control. Percentages of viable cells in biofilms were plotted by assuming 100% growth in water treated control.

Second, inhibition of biofilm formation. To evaluate the ability of peptides in inhibiting biofilm formation, E. coli E423–17 or A. baumannii B28–16 (105 CFU/mL) was prepared from the exponential phase. Aliquots of 180 μL of the bacterial suspension in TSB were added to each well of the microtiter plates containing 20 μL of various MIC folds (0.5× to 2× MIC) of YZ200 or colistin solutions. The plates were then incubated at 37 °C for 24 h. Media were then pipetted out and the wells were washed with 1× PBS to remove planktonic cells. To quantify the live cells within the biofilms, the XTT assay, as described previously39, was performed.

Third, Effects of peptides on established biofilms. Established biofilms are most difficult to eradicate. To evaluate the biofilm-disruptive ability, E. coli E423–17 or A. baumannii B28–16 was grown up in TSB media overnight. A second inoculation was made the next day to reach an exponential phase (OD600 ~0.3). Microtiter plates (96 wells, Corning Costar Cat No. 3595), after aliquoting with 180 μL of the culture to each well, were incubated at 37°C for 5 days to form biofilms in TSB. Media were aspirated post incubation and the attached biofilms were washed with 1× PBS to remove the planktonic bacteria. Each well was aliquoted with 20 μL of YZ200 or colistin solution and 180 μL of 10% fresh MHB, and plates were further incubated at 37°C for 24 h. Biofilms treated with water served as the positive control while media without bacterial inoculation served as the negative control. Live cells in the biofilms were quantitated using the XTT as described above. Absorbance was read at 450 nm (only media with XTT containing wells served as the blank) using a ChromateTM microtiter plate reader. Percentage biofilm growth (The plot legend is antibiofilm activity) for the peptides was plotted by assuming 100% biofilm growth in bacterial control alone. The data were represented as mean ± standard deviation, plots were generated using GraphPad prism 7, where * indicates p<0.05, ** p<0.01, and ***P<0.001, and ****p<0.0001 (one-way analyses of variance).

sec.title: Prediction of Peptide Activity, Toxicity, and 3D Structure.
sec.p: Peptide antibacterial activity and hemolytic toxicity were also predicted using three online machine learning prediction programs each. Peptide activity was predicted using antiBP2 (SVM, full sequence),21 AMPscanner v2 (www.dveltri.com/ascan),24 and AMPfun (fdblab.csie.ncu.edu.tw/AMPfun/index.html),23 respectively. Peptide hemolysis was predicted using HemoPred (codes.bio/Hemopred),25 HAPPENN (research.timmons.eu/happenn),26 and ToxinPred (http://crdd.osdd.net/raghava/toxinpred),27 respectively. Peptide 3D structure was predicted using both PEP-FOLD3 and the recently refined version PEP-FOLD4.44

sec.title: Statistical Analysis.
sec.p: The minimal inhibitory concentrations of peptides were expressed as ranges. Other data were analyzed using GraphPad Prism 7 (GraphPad Software, Inc., San Diego, CA, USA) and measured values were expressed as mean ± SD. One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was conducted by using Tukey’s honestly significant difference (HSD) test. Differences with P < 0.05 were considered statistically significant.
